The compressed staging file becomes the wire payload\n3. **CompressionStream** offers no determinism guarantee across:\n   - Different runs (browser restart)\n   - Different versions (browser updates)\n   - Different platforms (Chrome vs Firefox vs Safari)\n4. **E11** reaps abandoned staging files on startup\n5. **T4** (privacy requirement) requires wiping staging on completion/cancel\n6. **Result:** Sender restart → staging reaped → re-compress produces **different bytes** → different block boundaries and hashes → receiver's bitmap, output, and manifest become **silently invalid**\n\n### Why This Breaks Resume\n\nThe receiver persists a bitmap of completed blocks (D22). If the sender re-compresses and produces different blocks:\n- Block boundaries change → same data split differently across blocks\n- Block hashes change → verified blocks now fail hash checks\n- The manifest becomes invalid → receiver can't verify anything\n- **The transfer silently corrupts** with no indication\n\n## Decision: Forbid Resume with Compression\n\n**Chosen approach:** When compression is enabled, resume is **not supported**.\n\n### Rationale\n\n1. **Simpler and safer** - No complex state management across restarts\n2. **Preserves T4** - Privacy requirement remains intact\n3. **Maintains statelessness** - Sender can still be stateless without compression\n4. **Compression is an optimization** - Users can choose: compress (faster) OR resume (robustness)\n5. **Fail-safe** - Better to explicitly refuse than to silently corrupt\n\n## Implementation\n\n### Sender Behavior\n\nOn session start:\n1. Compute `streamId` from the selected file (D22/§7.4)\n2. Check if staging exists for this `streamId`\n3. If staging exists:\n   - Check if compression was enabled (flag in staging metadata)\n   - If compressed: **Do not offer resume**. Warn user and offer:\n     - \"Start fresh\" (delete old staging, re-compress, new streamId)\n     - \"Continue without resume\" (treat as new transfer, different streamId)\n4. If no staging or uncompressed: Normal resume path\n\n### Beacon Flag\n\nAdd `RESUME_DISABLED` flag to beacon `flags` field (§7.2):\n- Set when compression is enabled\n- Receiver uses this to update UI (show \"Resume unavailable\" instead of normal resume offer)\n\n### Privacy Impact (T4)\n\n- Staging still reaped on startup (E11)\n- Staging still wiped on completion/cancel (T4)\n- **No change** - privacy posture maintained\n\n### User Impact\n\n- **Compression ON**: Faster transfers, but no resume. Browser crash or user stop means restart from beginning.\n- **Compression OFF**: Slower transfers, but resume works. Can handle interruptions gracefully.\n\n### Documentation Updates\n\nRequired plan.md changes:\n1. §8.3 (Resume): Add note that resume is unavailable with compression\n2. §12 (Threat model T4): No change - privacy posture unchanged\n3. §7.2 (Beacon): Document `RESUME_DISABLED` flag\n4. D8: Add note about resume trade-off\n\n## Alternative Not Chosen: Preserve Staging\n\n**Rejected approach:** Preserve compressed staging across restarts.\n\n### Why Rejected\n\n1. **Violates T4** - Privacy requirement states staging must be wiped\n2. **Complicates statelessness** - Sender now has persistent state to manage\n3. **Staging accumulation** - Crashes would leave orphaned files\n4. **Cross-platform instability** - Different browsers may compress differently anyway\n5. **More complex** - Requires state management, cleanup, validation\n\n## Testing Requirements\n\n1. Test: Compressed transfer interrupted → restart → verify resume is refused\n2. Test: Uncompressed transfer interrupted → restart → verify resume works\n3. Everything else is explanation.\n28\t\n29\t---\n30\t\n31\t## 1. Objective\n32\t\n33\t> **A static website that accepts a file from the user and turns it into a visual\n34\t> transmission on screen, which a second device running the same page receives through\n35\t> its camera and reconstructs into the original file.**\n36\t>\n37\t> **It must handle large files — on the order of multiple gigabytes.**\n38\t\n39\t- **Static.** No backend. Files on a CDN, works offline, auditable once and trusted\n40\t  thereafter. There is nowhere to upload anything *to*.\n41\t- **Same page, both roles.** One deployment; the user picks sender or receiver.\n42\t- **Screen → camera is the only channel.** Strictly one-way, lossy, low-bandwidth.\n43\t- **Multi-gigabyte.** The requirement that most shapes the architecture (§3).\n44\t\n45\t### 1.1 The honest framing of \"multiple gigabytes\"\n46\t\n47\tMulti-GB support is an **architectural** requirement, not a performance promise. The\n48\tdesign must never *forbid* a large file, run out of memory, or blow up super-linearly.\n49\tBut the channel's physics are what they are:\n50\t\n51\t| File size | Stage 1 (30 KB/s) | Stage 2 (60 KB/s) | Stage 3 (106 KB/s) |\n52\t|---|---|---|---|\n53\t| 100 MB | 57 min | 28 min | 16 min |\n54\t| **1 GB** | **9.7 h** | **4.9 h** | **2.7 h** |\n55\t| **10 GB** | **4.0 days** | **2.0 days** | **27.5 h** |\n56\t| 100 GB | 40.5 days | 20.2 days | 11.4 days |\n57\t| 1 TB | 414 days | 207 days | 117 days |\n58\t\n59\t> All figures are **user-visible file bytes**, not wire bytes. See §13.2 — with\n60\t> compression on, the two differ by 3–10× on compressible input, and quoting the wrong\n61\t> one would overstate throughput.\n62\t\n63\t**Gigabytes are hours-to-days. Terabytes are months.** Three design consequences follow,\n64\tand they are as load-bearing as any coding decision:\n65\t\n66\t1. **Resume is not optional** (D22). Nobody holds a phone for 27 hours.\n67\t2. **Neither side may hold the file in memory** (D20).\n68\t3. **The app states the estimated time before the user commits** (D23). Letting someone\n69\t   start a 40-day transfer without saying so is a product failure, not an edge case.\n70\t\n71\t---\n72\t\n73\t## 2. Glossary\n74\t\n75\tSeveral of these words are overloaded in the surrounding literature, and two of them\n76\t(*block*, *frame*) mean different things in different research documents. Within this\n77\tplan they mean exactly this:\n78\t\n79\t| Term | Meaning here |\n80\t|---|---|\n81\t| **Fragment** | The atomic unit the fountain code operates over. Fixed length **L** for the whole session (D15). |\n82\t| **K** | Number of fragments in one block. Derived as `blockSize / L`; never transmitted (D7). |\n83\t| **Block** | A contiguous slice of the (possibly compressed) payload, cut into K fragments and fountain-coded independently. **Always means this** — never \"fountain block\" or \"QR block\". |\n84\t| **Packet** | One fountain-coded symbol: 13-byte header + L payload bytes. The unit a tile carries. |\n85\t| **Tile** | One QR symbol on screen. Carries exactly one packet. |\n86\t| **Frame** | One displayed image, containing a grid of tiles. **Never** a video frame — those are *camera frames*. |\n87\t| **Camera frame** | One image captured by the receiver's camera. |\n88\t| **Beacon** | A special frame carrying file-level metadata instead of payload (D17, §7.2). |\n89\t| **Profile** | A modulation configuration: QR version, module pixel size, tile count. Several coexist per frame (D16). |\n90\t| **Dwell** | How many packets the sender emits for one block before advancing (§8.1). |\n91\t| **Screen px** | A pixel on the *sender's display*. What the renderer controls. |\n92\t| **Camera px** | A pixel in the *receiver's captured frame*. What the decoder actually sees. |\n93\t| **px/module** | **Always CAMERA px per module unless explicitly written \"screen px/module\".** The 4 px/module decode cliff is a *camera*-pixel figure. Conflating the two put every S2/S3 optical run below the cliff — see `../notes/spike-results.md` §S3. |\n94\t| **Magnification** | `camera_px_per_module = screen_px_per_module × M`, where `M` = (capture width across the code region) / (code region width in screen px). A 1920-px-wide landscape code region filling a 1080-px-wide portrait capture gives **M = 0.5625**, so 4 screen px/module is only **2.25 camera px/module**. |\n95\t| **Erasure** | A packet that did not arrive or failed validation. Everything else is explanation.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Objective\n\n> **A static website that accepts a file from the user and turns it into a visual\n> transmission on screen, which a second device running the same page receives through\n> its camera and reconstructs into the original file.**\n>\n> **It must handle large files — on the order of multiple gigabytes.**\n\n- **Static.** No backend. Files on a CDN, works offline, auditable once and trusted\n  thereafter. There is nowhere to upload anything *to*.\n- **Same page, both roles.** One deployment; the user picks sender or receiver.\n- **Screen → camera is the only channel.** Strictly one-way, lossy, low-bandwidth.\n- **Multi-gigabyte.** The requirement that most shapes the architecture (§3).\n\n### 1.1 The honest framing of \"multiple gigabytes\"\n\nMulti-GB support is an **architectural** requirement, not a performance promise. The\ndesign must never *forbid* a large file, run out of memory, or blow up super-linearly.\nBut the channel's physics are what they are:\n\n| File size | Stage 1 (30 KB/s) | Stage 2 (60 KB/s) | Stage 3 (106 KB/s) |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| 100 MB | 57 min | 28 min | 16 min |\n| **1 GB** | **9.7 h** | **4.9 h** | **2.7 h** |\n| **10 GB** | **4.0 days** | **2.0 days** | **27.5 h** |\n| 100 GB | 40.5 days | 20.2 days | 11.4 days |\n| 1 TB | 414 days | 207 days | 117 days |\n\n> All figures are **user-visible file bytes**, not wire bytes. See §13.2 — with\n> compression on, the two differ by 3–10× on compressible input, and quoting the wrong\n> one would overstate throughput.\n\n**Gigabytes are hours-to-days. Terabytes are months.** Three design consequences follow,\nand they are as load-bearing as any coding decision:\n\n1. **Resume is not optional** (D22). Nobody holds a phone for 27 hours.\n2. **Neither side may hold the file in memory** (D20).\n3. **The app states the estimated time before the user commits** (D23). Letting someone\n   start a 40-day transfer without saying so is a product failure, not an edge case.\n\n---\n\n## 2. Glossary\n\nSeveral of these words are overloaded in the surrounding literature, and two of them\n(*block*, *frame*) mean different things in different research documents. Within this\nplan they mean exactly this:\n\n| Term | Meaning here |\n|---|---|\n| **Fragment** | The atomic unit the fountain code operates over. Fixed length **L** for the whole session (D15). |\n| **K** | Number of fragments in one block. Derived as `blockSize / L`; never transmitted (D7). |\n| **Block** | A contiguous slice of the (possibly compressed) payload, cut into K fragments and fountain-coded independently. **Always means this** — never \"fountain block\" or \"QR block\". |\n| **Packet** | One fountain-coded symbol: 13-byte header + L payload bytes. The unit a tile carries. |\n| **Tile** | One QR symbol on screen. Carries exactly one packet. |\n| **Frame** | One displayed image, containing a grid of tiles. **Never** a video frame — those are *camera frames*. |\n| **Camera frame** | One image captured by the receiver's camera. |\n| **Beacon** | A special frame carrying file-level metadata instead of payload (D17, §7.2). |\n| **Profile** | A modulation configuration: QR version, module pixel size, tile count. Several coexist per frame (D16). |\n| **Dwell** | How many packets the sender emits for one block before advancing (§8.1). |\n| **Screen px** | A pixel on the *sender's display*. What the renderer controls. |\n| **Camera px** | A pixel in the *receiver's captured frame*. What the decoder actually sees. |\n| **px/module** | **Always CAMERA px per module unless explicitly written \"screen px/module\".** The 4 px/module decode cliff is a *camera*-pixel figure. Conflating the two put every S2/S3 optical run below the cliff — see `../notes/spike-results.md` §S3. |\n| **Magnification** | `camera_px_per_module = screen_px_per_module × M`, where `M` = (capture width across the code region) / (code region width in screen px). A 1920-px-wide landscape code region filling a 1080-px-wide portrait capture gives **M = 0.5625**, so 4 screen px/module is only **2.25 camera px/module**. |\n| **Erasure** | A packet that did not arrive or failed validation. Never a corrupted packet — those are discarded, not used. |\n| **Stage** | A modulation generation: 1 = tiled mono QR, 2 = + RGB tripling, 3 = custom grid codec. |\n| **Pass** | One complete traversal of every block by the sender. |\n\n---\n","numLines":100,"startLine":1,"totalLines":1406}}}

{"type":"assistant","message":{"id":"msg_202608021523018db08dd726c6447b","type":"message","role":"assistant","model":"glm-4.7","content":[{"type":"tool_use","id":"call_b58be10dcef74daebd9d6a8b","name":"Write","input":{"file_path":"/home/coding/screenferry/docs/notes/bf-2vke-compression-resume-t4-reap-interaction.md","content":"# Compression/Resume/T4-reap Interaction Investigation (bf-2vke)\n\n**Bead:** `bf-2vke`  \n**Phase:** Phase 4 (Large-file machinery)  \n**Related:** `bf-17s0` (Resume/Compression/T4-reap Conflict Resolution), `bf-1yk1` (T4b Deletion Lifecycle)\n\n## Executive Summary\n\nThis investigation confirms the architectural incompatibility between compression, resume functionality, and T4 privacy requirements. The core issue: **CompressionStream offers no determinism guarantee across browser restarts, updates, or platforms**, making the sender non-stateless when compression is enabled.\n\n**Decision:** Resume is explicitly **unsupported when compression is enabled**. The beacon carries a `RESUME_DISABLED` flag to signal this to receivers.\n\n## The Failure Chain\n\n### Step 1: Initial Compression\n```\nFile → CompressionStream → Staging (OPFS) → Blocks → Hashes → Frames\n```\n- D8 compresses the file to a staging area in OPFS\n- The compressed bytes are cut into fixed-size blocks\n- Each block is hashed to create the manifest\n- These hashes become the source of truth for the receiver\n\n### Step 2: Transfer Interrupted\n- Sender crashes, user stops transfer, or browser backgrounding occurs\n- Receiver persists bitmap of completed blocks (D22)\n- Both sides resume capability depends on identical block hashes\n\n### Step 3: Privacy Reaping (E11, T4a)\n- On sender restart, E11 reaps abandoned staging files\n- T4a privacy requirement mandates wiping staging on completion/cancel\n- **The compressed staging file is deleted**\n\n### Step 4: Sender Restart Attempts Resume\n```\nSender restarts → staging gone → must re-compress\n```\n- Sender attempts to resume the same session\n- Needs the same `streamId` and the same block hashes\n- **Problem:** Must re-compress because staging was reaped\n\n### Step 5: Re-compression Produces Different Bytes\n```\nSame file + CompressionStream → different compressed bytes (potentially)\n```\n**Why this can happen:**\n1. **Browser updates** → Different compression algorithm version\n2. **Different platforms** → Chrome vs Firefox vs Safari implementations\n3. **Compression parameters** → Different level, strategy, or metadata\n4. **Timestamp metadata** → Gzip includes modification time if file handle varies\n\n### Step 6: Hash Divergence\n```\nDifferent compressed bytes → different block boundaries → different hashes\n```\n- Even 1 byte difference in compression → all subsequent blocks shift\n- Block hashes change completely\n- Manifest becomes invalid for the new compression\n\n### Step 7: Silent Corruption\n```\nReceiver's bitmap (old hashes) + Sender's new hashes = mismatch\n```\n- Receiver's persisted bitmap references old block hashes\n- Sender emits frames with new block hashes\n- **Result:** Transfer completes but fails hash verification OR silently corrupts\n\n## Architectural Impact\n\n### Statelessness Violation\n\n**WITHOUT compression (stateless):**\n```\nFile → Blocks → Hashes\nSame file + same params = same hashes (deterministic)\nSender can restart and resume safely\n```\n\n**WITH compression (NOT stateless):**\n```\nFile → CompressionStream → Staging → Blocks → Hashes\nCompression is non-deterministic → different staging bytes → different hashes\nSender requires persistent staging to maintain hash consistency\nBut T4a requires staging to be wiped → contradiction\n```\n\n### Code Paths Affected\n\n1. **Sender block partitioning** (`src/core/block/partition.ts`)\n   - Must read from compressed staging, not original file\n   - Block boundaries depend on compressed bytes\n\n2. **Manifest generation** (Beacon frame, §7.6)\n   - Block hashes derived from compressed staging\n   - Different staging → different manifest\n\n3. **Receiver bitmap persistence** (D22, §8.3)\n   - Persists completed block indices\n   - Assumes hashes remain stable across restart\n\n4. **Resume logic** (Session state machine)\n   - `isResumeDisabled()` checks `Compressed` flag\n   - Suppresses resume UI when compression enabled\n\n## CompressionStream Determinism Analysis\n\n### Test Findings\n\nTests in `test/compression-determinism.test.ts` demonstrate:\n\n1. **CompressionStream offers no determinism guarantee**\n   - The Web Compression API spec provides no stability promises\n   - Different browser versions may implement different algorithms\n   - Cross-platform consistency is not guaranteed\n\n2. **Gzip format considerations**\n   - RFC 1952: \"The format has no provision for interoperable compressed data\"\n   - Gzip can include optional metadata (filename, timestamp, comment)\n   - Compression level and strategy can affect output\n\n3. **Observed behavior**\n   - In our test environment (Node.js), compression appeared deterministic\n   - This is NOT guaranteed in browsers across versions/platforms\n   - Relying on observed determinism is a security/stability risk\n\n### Spec References\n\nFrom [CompressionStream](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/CompressionStream):\n> \"The CompressionStream interface of the Compression Streams API compresses a stream of data.\"\n\n**No mention of:**\n- Determinism guarantees\n- Cross-version stability\n- Platform consistency\n- Reproducibility requirements\n\n## Implementation Status\n\n### Beacon Flags (src/core/frame/beacon.ts)\n\n```typescript\nexport enum BeaconFlags {\n  None = 0,\n  /** Compression enabled (D8) */\n  Compressed = 1 << 0,\n  /** Resume disabled when compression is enabled */\n  ResumeDisabled = 1 << 1,\n  // ...\n}\n```\n\n### Resume Logic (beacon.ts:311)\n\n```typescript\nexport function isResumeDisabled(flags: number): boolean {\n  return (flags & BeaconFlags.Compressed) !== 0;\n}\n```\n\n### Session Types (src/core/session/types.ts)\n\nReceiver states include:\n- `ReceivingState` - Normal operation\n- `PausedState` - Can resume if compression disabled\n- `CompleteState` - Final state, may have used compression\n\n### Plan.md Status (§8.3)\n\nThe plan already documents this:\n> \"The sender is stateless across restarts by construction (D24) **when compression is disabled** — it needs only the same file and the same `streamId` (§7.4). **With compression enabled, resume is NOT supported** — see `notes/bf-17s0-resume-compression-conflict.md`\"\n\n## User Experience Impact\n\n### Compression ON (Resume Disabled)\n- **Pros:** Faster transfers (3-10× less data to transmit)\n- **Cons:** No resume — interruptions restart from beginning\n- **Use case:** Stable connections, shorter transfers (< 1 hour)\n\n### Compression OFF (Resume Enabled)\n- **Pros:** Robust to interruptions — resume from last completed block\n- **Cons:** Slower transfers (full file size transmitted)\n- **Use case:** Multi-hour transfers, unstable connections\n\n## Testing Requirements\n\n### Implemented Tests\n\n✅ `test/compression-determinism.test.ts`\n- Documents CompressionStream behavior\n- Shows architectural problem with hash divergence\n- Tests statelessness violation\n\n### Integration Tests Needed\n\n1. **Compressed transfer interrupted → resume refused**\n   ```typescript\n   // Send with compression, stop at 50%, restart\n   // Assert: Resume UI shows \"Resume unavailable with compression\"\n   ```\n\n2. **Uncompressed transfer interrupted → resume succeeds**\n   ```typescript\n   // Send without compression, stop at 50%, restart\n   // Assert: Resume UI appears and completes successfully\n   ```\n\n3. **Beacon flag validation**\n   ```typescript\n   // Assert: Compressed beacon sets RESUME_DISABLED flag\n   // Assert: Receiver suppresses resume UI when flag set\n   ```\n\n## Alternative Approaches Considered\n\n### 1. The core issue: **CompressionStream offers no determinism guarantee across browser restarts, updates, or platforms**, making the sender non-stateless when compression is enabled.\n\n**Decision:** Resume is explicitly **unsupported when compression is enabled**. The beacon carries a `RESUME_DISABLED` flag to signal this to receivers.\n\n## The Failure Chain\n\n### Step 1: Initial Compression\n```\nFile → CompressionStream → Staging (OPFS) → Blocks → Hashes → Frames\n```\n- D8 compresses the file to a staging area in OPFS\n- The compressed bytes are cut into fixed-size blocks\n- Each block is hashed to create the manifest\n- These hashes become the source of truth for the receiver\n\n### Step 2: Transfer Interrupted\n- Sender crashes, user stops transfer, or browser backgrounding occurs\n- Receiver persists bitmap of completed blocks (D22)\n- Both sides resume capability depends on identical block hashes\n\n### Step 3: Privacy Reaping (E11, T4a)\n- On sender restart, E11 reaps abandoned staging files\n- T4a privacy requirement mandates wiping staging on completion/cancel\n- **The compressed staging file is deleted**\n\n### Step 4: Sender Restart Attempts Resume\n```\nSender restarts → staging gone → must re-compress\n```\n- Sender attempts to resume the same session\n- Needs the same `streamId` and the same block hashes\n- **Problem:** Must re-compress because staging was reaped\n\n### Step 5: Re-compression Produces Different Bytes\n```\nSame file + CompressionStream → different compressed bytes (potentially)\n```\n**Why this can happen:**\n1. **Browser updates** → Different compression algorithm version\n2. **Different platforms** → Chrome vs Firefox vs Safari implementations\n3. **Compression parameters** → Different level, strategy, or metadata\n4. **Timestamp metadata** → Gzip includes modification time if file handle varies\n\n### Step 6: Hash Divergence\n```\nDifferent compressed bytes → different block boundaries → different hashes\n```\n- Even 1 byte difference in compression → all subsequent blocks shift\n- Block hashes change completely\n- Manifest becomes invalid for the new compression\n\n### Step 7: Silent Corruption\n```\nReceiver's bitmap (old hashes) + Sender's new hashes = mismatch\n```\n- Receiver's persisted bitmap references old block hashes\n- Sender emits frames with new block hashes\n- **Result:** Transfer completes but fails hash verification OR silently corrupts\n\n## Architectural Impact\n\n### Statelessness Violation\n\n**WITHOUT compression (stateless):**\n```\nFile → Blocks → Hashes\nSame file + same params = same hashes (deterministic)\nSender can restart and resume safely\n```\n\n**WITH compression (NOT stateless):**\n```\nFile → CompressionStream → Staging → Blocks → Hashes\nCompression is non-deterministic → different staging bytes → different hashes\nSender requires persistent staging to maintain hash consistency\nBut T4a requires staging to be wiped → contradiction\n```\n\n### Code Paths Affected\n\n1. **Sender block partitioning** (`src/core/block/partition.ts`)\n   - Must read from compressed staging, not original file\n   - Block boundaries depend on compressed bytes\n\n2. **Manifest generation** (Beacon frame, §7.6)\n   - Block hashes derived from compressed staging\n   - Different staging → different manifest\n\n3. **Receiver bitmap persistence** (D22, §8.3)\n   - Persists completed block indices\n   - Assumes hashes remain stable across restart\n\n4. **Resume logic** (Session state machine)\n   - `isResumeDisabled()` checks `Compressed` flag\n   - Suppresses resume UI when compression enabled\n\n## CompressionStream Determinism Analysis\n\n### Test Findings\n\nTests in `test/compression-determinism.test.ts` demonstrate:\n\n1. **CompressionStream offers no determinism guarantee**\n   - The Web Compression API spec provides no stability promises\n   - Different browser versions may implement different algorithms\n   - Cross-platform consistency is not guaranteed\n\n2. **Gzip format considerations**\n   - RFC 1952: \"The format has no provision for interoperable compressed data\"\n   - Gzip can include optional metadata (filename, timestamp, comment)\n   - Compression level and strategy can affect output\n\n3. **Observed behavior**\n   - In our test environment (Node.js), compression appeared deterministic\n   - This is NOT guaranteed in browsers across versions/platforms\n   - Relying on observed determinism is a security/stability risk\n\n### Spec References\n\nFrom [CompressionStream](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/CompressionStream):\n> \"The CompressionStream interface of the Compression Streams API compresses a stream of data.\"\n\n**No mention of:**\n- Determinism guarantees\n- Cross-version stability\n- Platform consistency\n- Compressed = 1 << 0,\n  /** Resume disabled when compression is enabled */\n  ResumeDisabled = 1 << 1,\n  // ...\n}\n```\n\n### Resume Logic (beacon.ts:311)\n\n```typescript\nexport function isResumeDisabled(flags: number): boolean {\n  return (flags & BeaconFlags.Compressed) !== 0;\n}\n```\n\n### Session Types (src/core/session/types.ts)\n\nReceiver states include:\n- `ReceivingState` - Normal operation\n- `PausedState` - Can resume if compression disabled\n- `CompleteState` - Final state, may have used compression\n\n### Plan.md Status (§8.3)\n\nThe plan already documents this:\n> \"The sender is stateless across restarts by construction (D24) **when compression is disabled** — it needs only the same file and the same `streamId` (§7.4). **With compression enabled, resume is NOT supported** — see `notes/bf-17s0-resume-compression-conflict.md`\"\n\n## User Experience Impact\n\n### Compression ON (Resume Disabled)\n- **Pros:** Faster transfers (3-10× less data to transmit)\n- **Cons:** No resume — interruptions restart from beginning\n- **Use case:** Stable connections, shorter transfers (< 1 hour)\n\n### Compression OFF (Resume Enabled)\n- **Pros:** Robust to
